sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Franklin County
sections.html:
Three offices split the work. The Auditor appraises every parcel and keeps ownership records, the Treasurer mails bills and takes payment, and the Board of Revision rules on value disputes. Pick the right one first and you save yourself a few transferred calls.

  • Auditor: 373 S. High Street, 21st floor, Columbus; phone 614-525-4663. Values, homestead applications, transfers and the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program.
  • Treasurer: 373 South High Street, 17th floor; phone 614-525-3438; counter hours are weekdays, 8 in the morning to 5 in the afternoon. Bills, payments, payment plans and the budget payment program.
  • Board of Revision: phone 614-525-3913, email BOR@franklincountyohio.gov. Complaints about appraised value.

The Auditor's real estate division oversees the appraisal of 483,319 parcels and processes more than $2 billion in tax collections for more than 85 entities countywide.

You can pay the annual bill in one installment early in the year, in two installments, or monthly. The first half falls in late February or early March, and the second half in July. For the 2026 collection the second-half date was July 20.

The first-half date moved in 2026, so go by the date printed on your own bill. A missing bill does not avoid penalty or interest. Ohio puts the duty on the parcel owner to get a bill in time to pay, and the Treasurer will send a duplicate by phone or online request at 614-525-3438.

Taxes are billed in arrears and can be paid only after the Auditor assesses them. The Budget Payment Program lets you prepay monthly into an escrow account in your name, which is applied automatically when the semi-annual bill comes due. Under Ohio Revised Code 7.16, the county posts its full tax rate listing on the Columbus Dispatch website.

Mail payments to the Franklin County Treasurer with the billing statement, and write the parcel number and a daytime phone number on the check. Enclose a stamped return envelope addressed to yourself if you want a receipt. The office has a kiosk for credit card payments through its secure payment site. A returned payment is reversed once the bank notifies the office, normally within two to three business days. There is no returned item fee, but a penalty can still apply if the due date was missed.

sections.h2: How the county values your house
sections.html:
Ohio law requires a reappraisal of all real property every six years, with an update at the three-year midpoint. Franklin County finished its countywide reappraisal in 2023 and a triennial update in 2026.

Between those cycles a value changes for only three reasons:

  • physical changes such as a new porch, patio or deck
  • demolition of a structure
  • a Board of Revision decision on a filed complaint

The bill is the tax rate times the value of the property, so a lower value flows straight to the bill. On the Treasurer's property search, the Distribution tab shows how your bill splits among the school district, municipality, library and other entities.

Complaints about value start with the Board of Revision. For tax year 2026 the Auditor's office accepts valuation complaints from November 20, 2026 until March 31, 2027.

The Board reviews the Auditor's appraised value and can change it based on evidence. A closing statement, a purchase contract or an appraisal all help. Hearings are held by Zoom, and you can request an in-person hearing at least 10 days ahead. Some cases go to mediation, which is less formal. The Board hears complaints about value only. The tax dollars you owe and the rate are outside its authority.

If you disagree with the ruling, you have 30 days from the date it was mailed to file a notice of appeal with the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or with the Court of Common Pleas. The notice must also go to the Board of Revision, and to the County Auditor for a court filing.

Each program has its own application:

  • Homestead exemption: for owners who turn 65 by the end of the application year, or are totally and permanently disabled as of January 1, and live in the home as a primary residence. A total income limit of $41,000 applies to applications tied to a 2025 return. Send applications to Franklin County Auditor, Homestead, 373 S High St, 21st Floor, or to homestead@franklincountyohio.gov.
  • Enhanced homestead exemption: for service members who are 100% disabled from service-connected injuries and for surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty. No income test applies, and approval reduces taxes on $50,000 of appraised value.
  • Current Agricultural Use Valuation (CAUV): farmland valued by soil type. Applications and renewals are due the first Monday of March.
  • Penalty remission: file form 23-A with the Treasurer's Office to ask that a late-payment penalty be forgiven.
  • Delinquent tax payment plans: the Treasurer offers plans to bring a past due account current.

Around 40,000 Franklin County parcels receive some tax incentive such as an abatement or a tax increment financing arrangement.

sections.h2: What a sale does to your taxes
sections.html:
An ownership change goes through the Auditor ahead of the Recorder. The county's conveyance fee is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, or $1 per $1,000 if the seller is receiving the homestead exemption. The transfer charge is $0.50 on every non-exempt transfer.

The buyer's statement of value must say whether the seller reported a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the home and whether the land was in farm use valuation (R.C. 319.202). When a reduction exists, buyer and seller account for the estimated amount between them. A farm use property that leaves the program can face a recoupment charge.

Since bills arrive in arrears, the closing statement is where buyer and seller divide the year. Ask the title agent for the current payment status from the Treasurer's property search, and ask the Treasurer about any penalty remission before closing. A seller who is behind can ask about a delinquent payment plan.

Back taxes do not prevent a sale, but they get paid from the proceeds. Look up the balance on the Treasurer's property search and phone 614-525-3438 for the payoff figure, which the title agent will request anyway. If you want the penalty reduced, file form 23-A before closing.

A cash buyer can close on a short timeline without waiting for a lender, which helps when a bill is already late. You still need the Auditor's transfer first, so line up the deed, the notary and both payments before you go downtown.

Franklin County is the center of the Columbus metropolitan area, with Columbus as county seat. The 2020 census counted 1,323,807 people, the most of any Ohio county, in 540,369 households. Delaware, Fairfield, Licking, Madison, Pickaway and Union counties border it.

A house in Dublin, Gahanna, Hilliard or Westerville is billed by the same county Treasurer, but the tax rate depends on the taxing districts that cover the parcel, such as the school district and municipality.

faqs.q: When is the second half of Franklin County property tax due?
faqs.a: The second half falls in July, and for the 2026 collection it was July 20. Taxes paid after the due date accrue penalty and interest, even if a bill never arrived.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Franklin County property value complaint?
faqs.a: With the Board of Revision through the Auditor's office. Tax year 2026 complaints are accepted from November 20, 2026 through March 31, 2027.

faqs.q: Which Franklin County office answers questions about a tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Treasurer at 614-525-3438. Value questions go to the Auditor at 614-525-4663, and complaints go to the Board of Revision at 614-525-3913.

faqs.q: Can I pay Franklin County property taxes monthly?
faqs.a: Yes. The Treasurer allows monthly installments and runs a Budget Payment Program that holds prepayments in an escrow account in your name and applies them to the bill.

faqs.q: Is the Franklin County conveyance fee lower for homestead sellers?
faqs.a: Yes. The fee falls from $3 to $1 per $1,000 of the sale price when the seller receives the homestead exemption at the time of transfer.
